newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Southern Africa teams up to tackle water problems.
newsitem.headline: Southern Africa teams up to tackle water problems.

text.p: Southern African countries are hoping that water problems, so often the source of division and conflict, will become the basis for cooperation and regional development.

The 12 South African Development Community (SADC) countries last year signed a document to cooperate in shared water basins to integrate the development of water supply with power generation, domestic water supply and other sectors.

"The idea is that at the end of it all, water will be a cause for cooperation rather than of conflict as water becomes scarcer," said Phera Ramoeli of the SADC's water sector, based in Maseru in the mountain kingdom of Lesotho.
He said the largely arid region could call on non-members such as Zaire, with an abundance of water, to help. SADC covers Africa south of Zaire.
"What we have is a protocol which outlines how best water can be utilised even if it means transferring water from regions of abundance to regions of need," he said.

Ramoeli said SADC members Angola and Mozambique, who until recently were fighting civil wars, had sufficient water but it was badly managed due to damaged infrastructure. Data on the changing characteristics of rivers in both countries was also long outdated, he said.
NAMIBIA IS DRIEST
Angola and its southern neighbour Namibia, driest country of the region, are studying a joint hydro-electric dam project on the shared Cunene river.
Namibian President Sam Nujoma and senior officials regularly visit the Angolan capital Luanda to push the project forward. Angola's parliament is currently studying reports for approval.
Mozambique has also teamed up with neighbouring South Africa, SADC's powerhouse, on its Cahora Bassaa hydro-electric dam project.
Mozambique currently spends about $10 million a year to buy electricity from South Africa but in April Mozambique will have the ability to export electicity for the first time in a decade.
The biggest combined water project of the region, the Lesotho Highlands Water Project that South Africa and the kingdom have been planning since the 1950s, is expected to become a reality in 1998.

Three months ahead of schedule, the project's first part is virtually complete and includes the Muela and Katse dams and transfer tunnels totalling 86 km (54 miles). Tenders for building the Mohale feeder dam will be put out at the end of the year.
The project diverts surplus water from Lesotho through tunnels to South Africa's industrial centre, Gauteng province which includes Johannesburg and Pretoria.
It will also provide hydro-electric power for Lesotho. Construction of a 72 megawatt hydropower station near the Muela Dam is underway and expected to be in commercial service in 1998.
The project, costing eight billion rand ($1.8 billion), is being funded by investment institutions in South Africa and Europe and the World Bank.
AFRICA'S HIGHEST DAM
The main reservoir, behind the Katse Dam, is already more than 60 percent full. The dam's walls rise 185 metres (607 feet), the highest in Africa.
"We will be testing water flows in the second half of this year. The official transfer of water is scheduled for January 1998," said project spokesman George van der Merwe.
South Africa and its landlocked eastern neighbour Swaziland are jointly building dams on the Komati river to boost agriculture through an expanded irrigation system.

Botswana, Nambia and Angola have formed a commission to discuss a plan by Namibia to take water from the shared Okavango river which feeds the Okavango delta, an ecological wonderland that drives Botswana's tourism industry.
That plan has alarmed ecologists but good rains since the start of 1997 in Nambia have eased water problems and could put the scheme on hold.
Peter van Niekerk of South Africa's water affairs department said the SADC water sector met for the first time early in February.
It will also tackle pollution. Van Niekert said it was not a serious problem but the sewage from villages built along rivers and from industrial areas had to be tackled.
"Although the sector is still in its infancy there is a great willingness to cooperate and now we will start seeing where the actual bottlenecks are," he told Reuters.
"It doesn't help just throwing money at projects, we need to pull together our resources to see where the constraints are so as to maximise the situation."
